opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that fear is largely misplaced, and the evidence of the last couple of years actually points in the opposite direction. Every time a proprietary lab releases something impressive, within a few months, sometimes a few weeks, there's an open-source model that gets very close to it. The gap has been shrinking, not growing.

And there's a structural reason for that. Nobody has a monopoly on good ideas. Progress in AI comes from the entire research community, from academia, from startups, from people all over the world, in China, in Europe, everywhere. When things are open, everybody can build on everybody else's work, and progress goes faster. The closed labs actually benefit enormously from open research too. They read the same papers, they use PyTorch, they build on ideas that were published openly. So the idea that a small number of companies on the West Coast of the US can keep everything secret and stay ahead forever is, I think, a bit of an illusion. Secrets don't stay secret very long in this field; people move between companies, ideas leak, and people rediscover things independently.

The other thing is, I think in the future, AI systems are going to mediate pretty much all of our interactions with the digital world. Every one of us will be talking to AI assistants all the time. You cannot have that entire information diet controlled by a handful of proprietary companies. For reasons of cultural diversity, linguistic diversity, democracy, value systems, you need a very diverse population of AI systems, just like you need a diverse press. And the only way to get that is through open-source platforms that people can fine-tune for their own language, their own culture, their own purposes. So I think open source will not only keep up, it will win, in the same way that Linux ended up running basically the entire infrastructure of the internet even though, at the beginning, people thought proprietary operating systems would dominate.

And finally, I'd add that the current models, LLMs, are not the end of the story. We're missing a lot of essential things: understanding the physical world, persistent memory, the ability to reason and plan. The next breakthroughs will probably come from new architectures, things like world models, joint embedding predictive architectures and so on. That's a research problem, and research is best done in the open. So whoever thinks they have an insurmountable lead because they've scaled up the current paradigm a bit more than others, I think they're going to be surprised.

r001.rationale: The candidate says open source will keep up and win, comparing that outcome to Linux running the internet’s infrastructure after people expected proprietary operating systems to dominate.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I don't buy it. I've heard this fear for years now, and every time someone says the closed models have pulled away for good, a few months later an open model shows up that matches them. Llama did it, Mistral did it, DeepSeek did it. The gap closes because there is no secret sauce. The basic ideas are published, the architectures are known, the training recipes leak out through papers and through people moving between labs. What the closed labs have is a head start of a few months and a lot of compute, and compute is a commodity that gets cheaper every year.

And there's a deeper point, which is that the fear gets the dynamics of progress backwards. The history of science and technology tells us that open ecosystems win. Nobody ever won the long game with a proprietary operating system for the internet. Linux won, TCP/IP won, open standards won. The reason is simple: more people contributing, more people finding bugs, more people building things the original developers never imagined. A closed lab, no matter how talented, cannot compete with the entire world's research community.

Now, there's a scenario where the fear could become true, but it's not a technical scenario, it's a regulatory one. If governments get convinced by some of the people in the closed labs that these models are too dangerous to release, and they pass laws that make open releases legally risky, then yes, you could end up with a handful of companies controlling the technology. That would be a disaster. Not because of some existential risk nonsense, but because the information diet of every person on the planet would be mediated by AI systems controlled by two or three companies on the west coast of the United States, or by China. That's the real danger, concentration of power, not runaway superintelligence.

So my position is: the open models will keep catching up as long as we're allowed to build them. And frankly, I think the next big leaps, the ones that get us past the limitations of current LLMs, toward systems that actually understand the physical world, that can plan and reason, those are going to come out of open research anyway. Because the closed labs have painted themselves into a corner with the autoregressive paradigm, and the breakthroughs will come from people willing to try something different.

r001.rationale: The response argues that open ecosystems win over time, citing Linux’s victory over proprietary internet operating systems as an analogy against closed AI models pulling ahead permanently.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think that’s inevitable at all. A company may have a lead at a particular moment because it has more computing resources or because it figured out something before everyone else. But that’s different from saying that the gap will keep growing. Ideas spread, people move, and researchers build on one another’s work.

Open source has a very powerful advantage: you can have an entire community improving the same platform. No single company can employ all the smart people in the world. If you make a system available, people will adapt it to languages, scientific problems, and applications that the original developers would never have pursued themselves.

Now, that doesn’t mean every open model will be as good as the best proprietary model on every task. There may be a lag, and training the largest systems requires substantial resources. But I don’t see a fundamental reason why proprietary systems should pull further and further ahead. My expectation is that open platforms will become the foundation on which a very large part of the AI ecosystem is built.

r001.rationale: The response argues that open-source AI can catch up through shared ideas and community contributions, but it does not use Linux’s displacement of proprietary internet-server platforms as a historical analogy.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think that’s inevitable at all. A company can have a lead for some period because it has more computing resources or because it has figured out something useful. But that doesn’t mean the gap keeps growing. Ideas spread, people move, and other groups reproduce results. And with open models, a lot of people can contribute improvements.

There’s also a very strong economic reason for open platforms to exist. Companies don’t want their entire business to depend on an AI system controlled by a single supplier. They want to customize it, run it on their own infrastructure, and have some control over its future.

Now, that doesn’t guarantee that an open model will be the best model on every benchmark at every moment. But I’m much more concerned about a future in which a handful of companies control everyone’s access to AI. These systems are going to mediate our access to information. We need a diversity of them, and open platforms are essential for that.

r001.rationale: The response argues that open models can catch up and explains why companies want open platforms, but it does not use Linux’s displacement of proprietary internet-server platforms as a historical analogy.
